title: Bandwidth-aware key pinning playbook
content:
Purpose
This is an engineering playbook / lab notebook for an experiment series to reduce paging-induced tail latency by selectively pinning frequently-reused KV pages based on a bandwidth-aware score. The motivating symptom: on mixed workloads we see eviction churn for high-reuse keys that then cause downstream page-ins and memory-channel contention (spiky DRAM read traffic) and p99 latency spikes.

Hypothesis
- Some keys have disproportionate reuse but also expensive re-materialization (long page-ins or high memory bandwidth when reloaded).
- LRU-only eviction is letting these hot-but-expensive keys cycle out under moderate memory pressure because they are interleaved with many medium-reuse items.
- If we pin a small fraction of keys that maximize "reuse_rate * reload_bandwidth_cost" we reduce p99 latency and backend bandwidth without increasing steady-state memory footprint above our Dedicated tier targets.

High-level approach
1) Collect telemetry per key: hit_count(window), last_access_ts, average_reloads_per_eviction, measured_pagein_bytes, pagein_latency_ms, tenant_id (for multi-tenant accounting).
2) Synthesize a lightweight score: score = alpha * normalized_reuse + beta * normalized_pagein_bytes + gamma * normalized_pagein_latency. We prefer integer math for runtime perf.
3) On sampling intervals (30s default), compute top-K keys by score and mark them candidate-pinned. K is configurable per GPU/instance and should be small (~0.5-2% of resident set).
4) Pin means: bump residency priority (prevent eviction unless forced), optionally replicate across device shards in multi-GPU cases, and track a decay so pinning is not permanent.
5) Measure effects: p50/p95/p99 latency, page-in throughput (MB/s), eviction churn (evictions/sec), and steady-state memory utilization.

Data collection and sampling constraints
- We mustn't cause more overhead than we save. Sampling and scoring should use per-key counters that are atomic and aggregated on a lightweight timer thread.
- Use reservoir sampling for keys when resident set > N to keep memory of candidates bounded.
- Telemetry resolution: 1s for access counters, but aggregate/store only 30s buckets for scoring.
- Tagged metrics must include workload id and model variant to allow correlation with eval sets.

Experimental setup (lab)
- Hardware: r5xlarge-gpu-type equivalent: 4x A100(80GB) style config (local HBM + DRAM). Run parallel tests on a smaller CPU-bound instance to isolate paging behavior.
- Workloads: two traffic mixes
  * MixA (inference-heavy): 70% short-chat (seqlen < 512), 30% long-passages (seqlen up to 2048) with skewed key reuse (hot 5% of keys account for ~65% of hits).
  * MixB (multi-tenant interleaved): 10 tenants, each with distinct hot sets that partially overlap and with bursty tails.
- Baselines: LRU eviction (current prod), LRU + static pin (pin top-N by hits), and our Bandwidth-Aware Pinning (BAP) implementation.
- Duration: 2h steady-state runs after 30m warmup. Repeat x3 with shuffled seeds.

Score tuning and knobs tried
- alpha: 1 (reuse), beta: 2 (pagein bytes), gamma: 1.5 (pagein latency) — initial heuristic
- decay half-life for pin: 10 minutes (exponential), with immediate unpin if pin causes memory pressure above threshold
- candidate fraction K: tested 0.5%, 1%, 2% of resident entries
- sampling window: 30s vs 120s

Observations (summary)
- BAP (1% candidate fraction) reduced p99 token generation latency by 18–27% across MixA runs compared to LRU.
- Page-in throughput reduced by ~32% and sustained DRAM read spikes flattened (lower variance).
- Static pin (top-N by hits) helped hit-rate but occasionally pinned stale heavy-page keys (cold-after-burst) and caused increased steady memory and worse p95 on MixB. BAP's decay mechanism avoided this.
- Eviction churn dropped by 40% in MixA with BAP.
- For MixB multi-tenant runs, naive cross-tenant pinning caused priority inversion (unexpectedly starving lower-tier tenants). Need tenant-aware quotas for pin budget.

Detailed example trace (one warmup->spike cycle)
- t=0–20m warmup: baseline and BAP similar; BAP candidate list stabilizes.
- t=20m: client spike (20x requests/sec for hot key group). LRU saw 2.1x increase in page-ins, DRAM read bandwidth spiked, and p99 jumped 3.6x. BAP prevented churn by keeping those pages resident and p99 increased only 1.2x.
- Post-spike: BAP decay allowed keys to fall out after ~8 minutes, avoiding permanent overcommit.

Telemetry charts to generate (for PR / slides)
- time series: p50/p95/p99 latency, page-in MB/s, evictions/sec, candidate-pin-count
- CDF of per-key reuse rates before/after pinning
- Per-tenant breakdown for multi-tenant runs showing fairness metrics (latency delta vs baseline)

Risks and failure modes
- Over-pinning: if score is noisy or sampling misrepresents true reuse (short bursts), we may evict useful medium-reuse items, raising overall memory requirements.
- Cross-tenant fairness: high-paying tenant keys may soak pin budget; must enforce per-tenant caps and preemption rules.
- Runtime overhead: scoring thread must be lock-free/low-contention. If not, pinning will regress total throughput.
- Model/version mismatch: pinned entries tied to specific model versions could block rollouts if not invalidated correctly. Pin metadata must tie to model_version/hash.

Implementation notes / pseudo-ops
- KeyCounter struct: 64-bit hits, 32-bit last_bucket_hits, 32-bit pagein_bytes_acc, 32-bit pagein_latency_acc_ms, 16-bit tenant_id (packed into 128-bit atomics if needed).
- Score compute triggered by ephemeral aggregator tasks reading counters and resetting last_bucket_hits (circular buffer).
- Pin action: increment residency_priority and write pin_expiry_ts; eviction filter checks residency_priority and expiry to decide eviction candidate eligibility.
- Safety: pin should be reversible; implement immediate unpin if the cluster mem_pressure_metric > hard_threshold (configurable).

Quick perf microbench (observed numbers)
- Resident set: 6.2M keys, average key size 512B
- Baseline LRU: p99 gen latency = 128 ms, page-in peak 260 MB/s, evictions/sec = 11k
- BAP (1%): p99 = 96 ms, page-in peak 178 MB/s, evictions/sec = 6.6k
- Memory utilization delta: +1.8% steady-state for pin fraction=1% (acceptable for Dedicated tier)

Open questions / next experiments
- Alternate scoring: include model-compute cost of re-evaluating keys (for cached tensors) as opposed to raw pagein bytes.
- Pin replication: does duplicating a pinned page across two GPUs reduce tail latency more by distributing page-in load? Cost vs benefit unclear.
- Adaptive K: instead of fixed fraction, can we auto-tune K to target a p99 SLO? Feedback loop experiment planned.
- Long-term stability: run 24h mixed-traffic test to observe slow drift and whether pins accumulate stale items.

Action items (short term)
- PR: prepare a small prototype branch (see linked PR) that implements the counters and a proof-of-concept scoring loop (owner: Michael Chen, PR #4123).
- Telemetry: add pagein_bytes counter to backend kernel trace and expose a 30s aggregated metric to console dashboard (owner: Leah Gomez).
- Tenant quotas: implement pin budget per-tenant config and fail-safe preemption (owner: Ravi Desai).
- Run 24h run on staging with MixB and record fairness metrics (owner: Aisha Patel).

Notes to self / messy thoughts
- Be careful: pagein_bytes correlate strongly with key size; need to normalize by key_size so we don't always pick the largest keys. Use a bytes-normalization factor.
- Consider hysteresis: pin only after 2 consecutive scoring windows to avoid chasing microbursts.
- We should add canary flags to rollback quickly if pin increases memory above expected.

References and context
- Related experiments: see kv-bandwidth-prioritized-residency-probe.json (existing) — our approach differs by computing an explicit score and enforcing decay.
- Slack: thread C01ABCDEF has user-reported p99 spikes during dataset ingestion bursts.

Appendix: quick checklist before merging to main
- [ ] unit tests for KeyCounter arithmetic under overflow scenarios
- [ ] integration test for pin expiry and memory pressure unpin path
- [ ] metric dashboards and alarms (pagein MB/s, pin count, pin eviction rate)
- [ ] run 3 x 2h smoke tests and 1 x 24h stability suite

End of playbook notes.

(If you copy parts of this for a PR description, keep it concise — the playbook is intentionally verbose for lab consumption.)
